title: Collecting Leaves
lead: Today in the Math Center we are going to play a game with colorful leaves, and a five frame. A five frame is a strip with 5 boxes in a row to help you count.
alt: Companion illustration of autumn leaves sorted on a table; it does not show a five frame or this class’s own work.
notes: Source and Teaching Materials

The weekly plan calls this activity Leaf Collections; the source lesson is titled Math: Collecting Leaves. The on-screen companion illustration shows leaves sorted on a table; it is not a five-frame demonstration or a photograph of this class’s work. Use the physical number cards or die, five frame, leaves, and book listed below for the demonstration.
Purpose
Children demonstrate one to one correspondence by adding leaves to a five frame .
Big Ideas
Color is a property of many natural and human-made things.
Colors can be mixed to make new colors.
Objective
I am learning to count objects to 5. (Learning Trajectories, p. 1-2)
Guiding Questions
What colors do we notice all around us?
How do colors provide information?
Family Engagement
Encourage families and caregivers to collect leaves with children. Encourage them to look at the leaves, notice the colors and count the number of leaves they find.
Vocabulary
less: a smaller amount than something else
more: a bigger amount than something else
equal: the same amount as something else
Materials and Preparation
Goodbye Summer, Hello Autumn, Kenard Pak
Flag a page with autumn leaves in the illustration.
number dot cards 0-5 or dice 0-5 enough for each child at the center (see Week 1)
blank 5 frame, one for each child
Cut out.
leaf template
Cut out the leaves. Make enough so that each child could have up to 5.
Building Blocks Teacher’s Guide pg. 104 week 7
Intro to Centers
Today in the Math Center we are going to play a game with colorful leaves, and a five frame. A five frame is a strip with 5 boxes in a row to help you count.
Hold up the five frame.

These leaves are similar to the leaves in Goodbye Summer, Hello Autumn. The leaves in the story are green, red, yellow, and brown. Just like the leaves we are going to use today to play a game in the math center.
First we are going to pull a Number Card from the pile (or roll a die). What number is this? How did you know this was a ____? Let’s count to make sure it is a _____?
Count out loud with children.
Now we are going to add that many leaves/leaf to our five frame. Let’s count as we add them to five frame.
What if we want one more leaf on the tree? More means a bigger amount than something else. What can we do?
Harvest children’s ideas.
What If we want one less leaf on the tree? Less means a smaller amount of something. What can we do?
Harvest children’s ideas.
What if I want the same amount as my friend _____? The same amount is equal. They have 1 and I want 1. What can I do?
Harvest children’s ideas.
We will play this game at the Math Center.
During Centers
Encourage children to pull a card or roll a die. Have them count to see how many they will add to their five frame. Then count the leaves to see if it is the same as the card they pulled.
Differentiation Ideas
Count using lower numbers (0-5).
Use larger sized objects or felt for leaves.
Place velcro on the leaves and where they go (on 5-frame and/or tree) so that they stay in place when children are counting.
Use 5-frame cards with or without numerals (0-5).
For a more tactile 5-frame, use wiki sticks or craft sticks to demarcate the lines on the 5-frame or cut an egg cart down to 5 spaces.
Use the tree templates pre-marked with spaces for leaves on the tree (located in the adapted resource folder).
Say the number without showing the card.
As an extension, count up to higher numbers (5-10).
Facilitation
How many leaves do you have on your five frame? How do you know?
What if you added one more, how many do you have on your five frame now?
Do you have more or less than ______? How do you know?
Standards
PreK.SEL7 The child will demonstrate the ability to communicate with others in a variety of ways.
PreK.APL4 The child will demonstrate creativity in thinking and use of materials.
PK.CC.A Know number names and the counting sequence.
1. Listen to and say the names of numbers in meaningful contexts

title: Multilingual Color Poem or Book
lead: Today we will write our own book [or poem] using the color words we know in our languages.
alt: Original Favorite Objects visual support with a menu of favorite objects and color choices.
notes: Source Examples and Classroom Languages

The names, objects, and languages in the source poem below are fictional teaching examples, not information about children in this class. Use the children’s actual contributions and family-supported color words; do not infer the languages spoken in this classroom from the examples.

Use the source’s monolingual alternative when applicable: name the language spoken and some other languages spoken by others in the school community. The source’s statements about a multilingual classroom apply only when that describes the class.

The on-screen image is the original Favorite Objects visual support, provided to help children choose an object and a color. It is not a finished class poem or book. Use a physical copy of the chosen book, prepared color cards, and the children’s own drawings for the activity.
Purpose
Children write a poem or book together using color words in the languages they speak.
Big Ideas
Color is a property of many natural and human-made things.
We can all communicate about colors.
Guiding Question
What colors do we notice all around us?
How can we explore and communicate ideas and feelings through colors?
Family Engagement
Invite families to share the names of colors in their languages. Create cards or a list of the color names for each language spoken by children and teachers in the class.
Vocabulary
favorite: the one you like the most
multilingual: knowing more than one or many languages
poem: a piece of writing that can rhyme and usually expresses imagination and emotion
Color words in languages spoken by children in the class (e.g. Spanish: azul: blue amarillo: yellow rojo:red)
Materials and Preparation
Green Is a Chile Pepper or Red is a Dragon, Roseanne Thong
chart paper
markers
poem example
If creating a poem, write the poem on the chart paper.
Green Is a Chile Pepper visual glossary, from Week 2, Read Aloud
Favorite Objects visual (optional)
Gather the names of colors in the languages spoken in the class. Ask families to support or use online resources such as Google Translate.
Decide if you want to create a class poem or a class book. If a poem, see the example below. If creating a book, children can create individual or shared pages to contribute.
Poem Example — Fictional Source Examples
Our Favorite Colors
[use this pattern to create a class poem using the children’s names and favorite items]
We love colors in all our languages!
Maya loves blue flowers - azul (Spanish)
María loves yellow butterflies - amarelo (Portuguese)
Iman loves green trains - أخضر (pronounced akhdar - Arabic)
…[continue for all children in the class]
We love colors in all our languages!
Intro to Centers
In Green is a Chile Pepper, all of the color words are written in two languages, English and Spanish.
Look through the book and read some of the words together.
In our classroom, we speak many different languages.
If the classroom is monolingual, name the language spoken and some other languages spoken by others in the school community.
What language do you speak with your family?
Invite children to share and support them if they are unsure. Teachers can also share the languages they speak.
Having more than one language in our classroom is amazing, our community is multilingual.

Today we will write our own book [or poem] using the color words we know in our languages. You can add the name of your favorite color in your language or a language you are excited about. We can also draw pictures of things that are that color to illustrate our poem.
During Centers
Invite children to look at the multilingual color cards and notice the different ways to say the names of the colors. Read some of the color names and track print while reading.
Invite children to add their own line to the poem or page to the book, by choosing a language and a favorite color/object to include.
Invite children to create illustrations for the poem or book page. If writing a poem, the illustrations can be made on small pieces of paper, and cut/glued around the edges of the poem to decorate.
Read the poem/book back to the children as it is created.
Differentiation Ideas
Add in more words in children’s home languages, if known (i.e. not just the color word but also objects or feelings).
Use the favorite objects communication support (see below) to support children with choosing an object and its color.
Invite children to select their favorite color from a set of color cards or from objects around the room, providing them the word in English or another language.
Facilitation
What is your favorite color? Why do you like it the most?
How do you say [color name] in your language?
What is something you love that is (blue, red…)? Why do you love it?
How will you draw your [red balloon…] to illustrate our poem/book?
How is the way you say yellow in [Spanish] different from [Arabic]?
Extensions

Encourage children to join you in reading the poem/book or tracking print while you read aloud. Rather than expecting them to read all the words, focus their attention on their own and their friends’ names, which they might recognize in print.
Make printed copies of the finished poem or book to send home so that children can share and read with their families.
Read the poem or book in the end-of-unit celebration.
Standards
W.PreK.1 Dictate words to express a preference or opinion about a topic (e.g., “I would like to go to the fire station to see the truck and meet the firemen.”).
W.PreK.2 Use a combination of dictating and drawing to supply information about a topic.
RL.PreK.9 With prompting and support, make connections between a story or poem and their own experiences.
PreK.SEL7 The child will demonstrate the ability to communicate with others in a variety of ways.
